text: Now run SMC algorithm fit model: default values number particles, Markov chain steps, learning rate can somewhat conservative, depending application. 34 peaks 2401 wavenumbers, fitting model can take fair amount time, even running parallel 8 CPU cores: downside choosing smaller values tuning parameters run risk SMC collapsing. quality particle distribution deteriorates iteration, measured effective sample size (ESS):  SMC collapses, best solution increase number particles run . Thus, choosing conservative number begin sensible strategy. 8000 particles maximum 60 MCMC steps per SMC iteration, can see plots algorithm converged target distribution. detailed convergence diagnostics can obtained genealogical history particles Lee Whiteley (2015), yet implemented R package.
code: data("result", package = "serrsBayes") if(!exists("result")) {   t1 <- Sys.time()   result <- fitVoigtPeaksSMC(wavenumbers, spectra, priors, mcSteps=50, minPart = 7900, npart = 8000)   result$time <- Sys.time() - t1   save(result, file="Figure 2/result.rda") } print(paste(format(result$time,digits=4)," for",length(result$ess),"SMC iterations.")) #> [1] "3.553 hours  for 254 SMC iterations." plot.ts(result$ess, ylab="ESS", main="Effective Sample Size",         xlab="SMC iteration", ylim=c(0,max(result$ess))) abline(h=max(result$ess)/2, col=4, lty=2) abline(h=0,lty=2) plot.ts(result$accept, ylab="accept", main="M-H Acceptance Rate",         xlab="SMC iteration", ylim=c(0,max(result$accept))) abline(h=0.234, col=4, lty=2) abline(h=0,lty=2) plot.ts(result$times/60, ylab="time (min)", main="Elapsed Time", xlab="SMC iteration") plot.ts(result$kappa, ylab=expression(kappa), main="Likelihood Tempering",         xlab="SMC iteration") abline(h=0,lty=2) abline(h=1,lty=3,col=4)

title: Introducing serrsBayes
text: subsample particles can used plot posterior distribution baseline peaks:  Notice uncertainty baseline greatest peaks bunched close together, exactly expect. also reflected uncertainty spectral signature. can compute Voigt parameters full width half maximum (FWHM) peak: Finally, display lower upper 95% highest posterior density (HPD) intervals parameters peak: 95% highest posterior density intervals pseudo-Voigt peaks
code: samp.idx <- sample.int(length(result$weights), 50, prob=result$weights) samp.mat <- resid.mat <- matrix(0,nrow=length(samp.idx), ncol=nWL) samp.sigi <- samp.lambda <- numeric(length=nrow(samp.mat)) samp.loc <- colMeans(result$location) spectra <- as.matrix(spectra) plot(wavenumbers, spectra[1,], type='l', xlab=expression(paste("Raman shift (cm"^{-1}, ")")), ylab="Intensity (a.u.)") for (pt in 1:length(samp.idx)) {   k <- samp.idx[pt]   samp.mat[pt,] <- mixedVoigt(result$location[k,], result$scale_G[k,],                               result$scale_L[k,], result$beta[k,], wavenumbers)   samp.sigi[pt] <- result$sigma[k]   samp.lambda[pt] <- result$lambda[k]      Obsi <- spectra[1,] - samp.mat[pt,]   g0_Cal <- length(Obsi) * samp.lambda[pt] * result$priors$bl.precision   gi_Cal <- crossprod(result$priors$bl.basis) + g0_Cal   mi_Cal <- as.vector(solve(gi_Cal, crossprod(result$priors$bl.basis, Obsi)))    bl.est <- result$priors$bl.basis %*% mi_Cal # smoothed residuals = estimated basline   lines(wavenumbers, bl.est, col=2)   lines(wavenumbers, bl.est + samp.mat[pt,], col=4)   resid.mat[pt,] <- Obsi - bl.est[,1] } title(main="Baseline for TAMRA") rug(samp.loc, col=4,lwd=2)  plot(range(wavenumbers), range(samp.mat), type='n', xlab=expression(paste("Raman shift (cm"^{-1}, ")")), ylab="Intensity (a.u.)") abline(h=0,lty=2) for (pt in 1:length(samp.idx)) {   lines(wavenumbers, samp.mat[pt,], col=4) } title(main="Spectral Signature") rug(samp.loc,col=4,lwd=2) result$voigt <- result$FWHM <- matrix(nrow=nrow(result$beta), ncol=ncol(result$beta)) for (k in 1:nrow(result$beta)) {   result$voigt[k,] <- getVoigtParam(result$scale_G[k,], result$scale_L[k,])   f_G <- result$scale_G[k,]   f_L <- result$scale_L[k,]   result$FWHM[k,] <- 0.5346*f_L + sqrt(0.2166*f_L^2 + f_G^2) }

title: Methanol example
text: first step always read spectrum plot . Normally use R package hyperSpec , data going use included R package serrsBayes:
code: library(serrsBayes) data("methanol", package = "serrsBayes") wavenumbers <- methanol$wavenumbers spectra <- methanol$spectra  peakLocations <- c(1033, 1106, 1149, 1448) nPK <- length(peakLocations) pkIdx <- numeric(nPK) for (i in 1:nPK) {   pkIdx[i] <- which.min(wavenumbers < peakLocations[i]) } nWL <- length(wavenumbers) plot(wavenumbers, spectra[1,], type='l', col=4,      xlab=expression(paste("Raman shift (cm"^{-1}, ")")), ylab="Intensity (a.u.)", main="Observed Raman spectrum for methanol") points(peakLocations, spectra[1,pkIdx], cex=2, col=2) text(peakLocations + c(100,20,40,0), spectra[1,pkIdx] + c(0,700,400,700), labels=peakLocations)

title: Methanol example
text: can use exactly priors given package README: can see problem model fit:  Adjusting priors going fix . underlying issue peak location 1448 cm−1^{-1} doesn’t match observed data. Even small difference location one peaks can adversely effect entire model fit. kind issue function fitVoigtPeaksSMC designed handle.
code: lPriors <- list(scale.mu=log(11.6) - (0.4^2)/2, scale.sd=0.4, bl.smooth=10^11, bl.knots=50,                  beta.mu=5000, beta.sd=5000, noise.sd=200, noise.nu=4) tm <- system.time(result <- fitSpectraSMC(wavenumbers, spectra, peakLocations, lPriors)) print(paste(tm["elapsed"]/60, "minutes")) ## [1] "54.2650666666667 minutes" samp.idx <- sample.int(length(result$weights), 200, prob=result$weights) plot(wavenumbers, spectra[1,], type='l', lwd=3,      xlab=expression(paste("Raman shift (cm"^{-1}, ")")), ylab="Intensity (a.u.)", main="Fitted model with Lorentzian peaks") for (pt in samp.idx) {   bl.est <- result$basis %*% result$alpha[,1,pt]   lines(wavenumbers, bl.est, col="#C3000009")   lines(wavenumbers, bl.est + result$expFn[pt,], col="#00C30009") }

code: lPriors2 <- list(loc.mu=peakLocations, loc.sd=rep(50,nPK), scaG.mu=log(16.47) - (0.34^2)/2,                  scaG.sd=0.34, scaL.mu=log(25.27) - (0.4^2)/2, scaL.sd=0.4, noise.nu=5,                  noise.sd=50, bl.smooth=1, bl.knots=50) data("result2", package = "serrsBayes") if(!exists("result2")) {   tm2 <- Sys.time()   result2 <- fitVoigtPeaksSMC(wavenumbers, spectra, lPriors2, npart=3000, rate=0.499,mcSteps=50)   result2$time <- Sys.time() - tm2   save(result2, file="Figure 2/result2.rda") } print(paste(format(result2$time), "for",length(result2$ess),"SMC iterations.")) ## [1] "7.083923 mins for 19 SMC iterations." samp.idx <- 1:nrow(result2$location) plot(wavenumbers, spectra[1,], type='l', lwd=3,      xlab=expression(paste("Raman shift (cm"^{-1}, ")")), ylab="Intensity (a.u.)", main="Fitted model with Voigt peaks") samp.mat <- resid.mat <- matrix(0,nrow=length(samp.idx), ncol=nWL) samp.sigi <- samp.lambda <- numeric(length=nrow(samp.mat)) for (pt in 1:length(samp.idx)) {   k <- samp.idx[pt]   samp.mat[pt,] <- mixedVoigt(result2$location[k,], result2$scale_G[k,],                               result2$scale_L[k,], result2$beta[k,], wavenumbers)   samp.sigi[pt] <- result2$sigma[k]   samp.lambda[pt] <- result2$lambda[k]      Obsi <- spectra[1,] - samp.mat[pt,]   g0_Cal <- length(Obsi) * samp.lambda[pt] * result2$priors$bl.precision   gi_Cal <- crossprod(result2$priors$bl.basis) + g0_Cal   mi_Cal <- as.vector(solve(gi_Cal, crossprod(result2$priors$bl.basis, Obsi)))    bl.est <- result2$priors$bl.basis %*% mi_Cal # smoothed residuals = estimated basline   lines(wavenumbers, bl.est, col="#C3000009")   lines(wavenumbers, bl.est + samp.mat[pt,], col="#00C30009")   resid.mat[pt,] <- Obsi - bl.est[,1] } for (j in 1:nPK) {   hist(result2$location[,j], main=paste("Peak",j),        xlab=expression(paste("Peak location (cm"^{-1}, ")")),        freq=FALSE, xlim=range(result2$location[,j], peakLocations[j]))   lines(density(result2$location[,j]), col=4, lty=2, lwd=3)   abline(v=peakLocations[j], col=2, lty=3, lwd=3) }

title: Methanol example
text: can use posterior fitVoigtPeaksSMC obtain priors running fitSpectraSMC. can useful, example, fitting model multiple datasets obtained experimental conditions. first question whether use Lorentzian Gaussian broadening functions. can transform posteriors ψG\psi_G ψL\psi_L obtain number η\eta 0 1 peak, 0 implies pure Gaussian 1 implies Lorentzian. Wikipedia page provides equations (Thompson et al. 1987): $$ f_G = 2\psi_G\sqrt{2\log\{2\}} \\ f_L = 2\psi_L \\ f_V \approx 0.5346 f_L + \sqrt{0.2166f_L^2 + f_G^2} \\ f_{total} \approx \left(f_G^5 + 2.69269f_G^4 f_L + 2.42843f_G^3 f_L^2 + 4.47163f_G^2 f_L^3 + 0.07842f_G f_L^4 + f_L^5 \right)^{1/5} \\ \eta \approx 1.33603 \frac{f_L}{f_{total}} - 0.47719 \left(\frac{f_L}{f_{total}} \right)^2 + 0.11116 \left(\frac{f_L}{f_{total}} \right)^3 $$ equations implemented function getVoigtParam:  two largest peaks definitely look Lorentzian, uncertainty line shape smaller peaks. gives us confidence fitSpectraSMC able give us good fit data, long get peak locations closer correct values. can also use moment matching set informative priors amplitudes:
code: nPart <- nrow(result2$beta) result2$voigt <- result2$FWHM <- matrix(nrow=nPart, ncol=nPK) for (k in 1:nPart) {   result2$voigt[k,] <- getVoigtParam(result2$scale_G[k,], result2$scale_L[k,])   f_G <- 2*result2$scale_G[k,]*sqrt(2*log(2))   f_L <- 2*result2$scale_L[k,]   result2$FWHM[k,] <- 0.5346*f_L + sqrt(0.2166*f_L^2 + f_G^2) } for (j in 1:nPK) {   hist(result2$voigt[,j], main=paste("Peak",j),        xlab=expression(eta), freq=FALSE, xlim=c(0,1))   lines(density(result2$voigt[,j]), col=4, lty=2, lwd=3) } lPriors3 <- list(scale.mu=log(11.6) - (0.4^2)/2, scale.sd=0.4, bl.smooth=10^11, bl.knots=50, noise.sd=200, noise.nu=4) lPriors3$beta.mu <- mean(result2$beta) lPriors3$beta.sd <- sd(result2$beta) pkLocNew <- c(colMeans(result2$location), 1550) tm3 <- system.time(result3 <- fitSpectraSMC(wavenumbers, spectra, pkLocNew, lPriors3, npart=2000)) print(paste(tm3["elapsed"]/60, "minutes")) ## [1] "28.6862833333333 minutes" samp.idx <- sample.int(length(result3$weights), 200, prob=result3$weights) plot(wavenumbers, spectra[1,], type='l', lwd=3,      xlab=expression(paste("Raman shift (cm"^{-1}, ")")), ylab="Intensity (a.u.)", main="Fitted model with informative priors") for (pt in samp.idx) {   bl.est <- result3$basis %*% result3$alpha[,1,pt]   lines(wavenumbers, bl.est, col="#C3000009")   lines(wavenumbers, bl.est + result3$expFn[pt,], col="#00C30009") } rug(pkLocNew, col=4, lwd=2)

title: Bayesian Modelling of Raman Spectroscopy
text: serrsBayes provides model-based quantification surface-enhanced resonance Raman spectroscopy (SERRS) using sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) algorithms. details Bayesian model informative priors provided Moores et al. (2026) “Bayesian modelling quantification Raman spectroscopy.,” published 2025 MATRIX Annals, Part II (Springer). Development software supported UK Engineering & Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC) programme grant “Situ Nanoparticle Assemblies Healthcare Diagnostics Therapy” (ref: EP/L014165/1).

title: Bayesian Modelling of Raman Spectroscopy
text: simulate synthetic Raman spectrum known parameters:  Fit model using SMC: Sample 200 particles posterior distribution:
code: set.seed(1234) library(serrsBayes)  wavenumbers <- seq(700,1400,by=2) spectra <- matrix(nrow=1, ncol=length(wavenumbers)) peakLocations <- c(840,  960, 1140, 1220, 1290) peakAmplitude <- c(11500, 2500, 4000, 3000, 2500) peakScale <- c(10, 15, 20, 10, 12) signature <- weightedLorentzian(peakLocations, peakScale, peakAmplitude, wavenumbers) baseline <- 1000*cos(wavenumbers/200) + 2*wavenumbers spectra[1,] <- signature + baseline + rnorm(length(wavenumbers),0,200) plot(wavenumbers, spectra[1,], type='l', xlab=expression(paste("Raman shift (cm"^{-1}, ")")), ylab="Intensity (a.u.)") lines(wavenumbers, baseline, col=2, lty=4) lines(wavenumbers, baseline + signature, col=4, lty=2, lwd=2) lPriors <- list(scale.mu=log(11.6) - (0.4^2)/2, scale.sd=0.4, bl.smooth=10^11, bl.knots=50,                  beta.mu=5000, beta.sd=5000, noise.sd=200, noise.nu=4) tm <- system.time(result <- fitSpectraSMC(wavenumbers, spectra, peakLocations, lPriors)) print(tm) #>    user  system elapsed  #> 164.263   1.925  43.341 samp.idx <- sample.int(length(result$weights), 200, prob=result$weights) plot(wavenumbers, spectra[1,], type='l', xlab=expression(paste("Raman shift (cm"^{-1}, ")")), ylab="Intensity (a.u.)") for (pt in samp.idx) {   bl.est <- result$basis %*% result$alpha[,1,pt]   lines(wavenumbers, bl.est, col="#C3000009")   lines(wavenumbers, bl.est + result$expFn[pt,], col="#0000C309") }

code: wavenumbers <- seq(200,600,by=10) spectra <- matrix(nrow=1, ncol=length(wavenumbers)) peakLocations <- c(300,500) peakAmplitude <- c(10000,4000) peakScale <- c(10, 15) signature <- weightedLorentzian(peakLocations, peakScale, peakAmplitude, wavenumbers) baseline <- 1000*cos(wavenumbers/200) + 2*wavenumbers spectra[1,] <- signature + baseline + rnorm(length(wavenumbers),0,200) lPriors <- list(scale.mu=log(11.6) - (0.4^2)/2, scale.sd=0.4, bl.smooth=10^11, bl.knots=20,                 amp.mu=5000, amp.sd=5000, noise.sd=200, noise.nu=4) rw_bw <- c(100, 100, 2, 2) result <- fitSpectraMCMC(wavenumbers, spectra, peakLocations, lPriors, rw_bw, 500) #> [1] "MCMC with 1 observations of 2 peaks at 41 wavenumbers." #> [1] "Step 0: computing 20 B-spline basis functions took 0.0379999999999994 sec." #> [1] "Step 1: initialization took 0.00100000000000033 sec for 4 parallel chains." result$n_acc #> [1] 769

title: Compute the pseudo-Voigt mixing ratio for each peak. — getVoigtParam
text: First, calculate polynomial average scale parameters according approximation Thompson et al. (1987): $$f_{G,L} = (\sigma_j^5 + 2.69\sigma_j^4\phi_j + 2.42\sigma_j^3\phi_j^2 + 4.47\sigma_j^2\phi_j^3 + 0.07\sigma_j\phi_j^4 + \phi_j^5)^{1/5} $$ Voigt mixing parameter \(\eta_j\) defined : $$\eta_j = 1.36\frac{\phi_j}{f_{G,L}} - 0.47(\frac{\phi_j}{f_{G,L}})^2 + 0.11(\frac{\phi_j}{f_{G,L}})^3$$

what: Bayesian modelling and quantification of Raman spectroscopy — serrsBayes-package
title: Bayesian modelling and quantification of Raman spectroscopy — serrsBayes-package
text: R package implements sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) algorithms fitting generalised additive mixed model (GAMM) Raman spectra. multivariate observations highly collinear lend reduced-rank representation.  GAMM separates hyperspectral signal three components: sequence Lorentzian Gaussian peaks; smoothly-varying baseline; zero-mean, additive white noise. parameters component model estimated iteratively using SMC. posterior distributions parameters given observed spectra represented population weighted particles.

title: Bayesian modelling and quantification of Raman spectroscopy — serrsBayes-package
text:
Raman spectroscopy can used identify molecules characteristic scattering light laser. pattern peaks Raman spectrum corresponds vibrational modes molecule. shift wavenumber photons proportional change energy state, reflected locations peaks. Surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) technique amplifies Raman signal using metallic substrates, nanoparticles. laser can also tuned resonant frequency molecule, known surface-enhanced resonance Raman scattering (SERRS). controlled experimental conditions, amplitudes peaks linearly related concentration molecule, limit detection (LOD) monolayer coverage nanoparticle surface. GAMM represents peaks baseline continuous functions. background fluorescence modelled using penalised cubic spline, peaks additive mixture squared exponential (Gaussian) Lorentzian (Cauchy) kernels: $$Y = \sum_{m=1}^M \alpha_{,m}B_m(
u_j) + \sum_{p=1}^P s(
u_j | l_p, A_p, \phi_p) + \epsilon_{,j}$$ \(Y\) matrix hyperspectral observations \(y_{,j}\) discretised wavenumbers \(
u_j\); \(B_m\) \(M\) spline basis functions coefficients \(\alpha_{,m}\); \(s(
u_j | l_p, A_p, \phi_p)\) radial basis functions peak, location \(l_p\), amplitude \(A_p\), scale \(\phi_p\) parameters. \(\epsilon_{,j}\) assumed zero mean, additive white noise constant variance \(\sigma^2\). model-based approach accounts differences resolution experimental conditions, enabling comparison alignment heterogeneous spectra. relationship concentration peak intensity can quantified fitting Bayesian functional regression: $$A_p = c_i  eta_p$$ \(c_i\) nanomolar (nM) concentration molecule \(\)th spectrum, \(c_{LOD} < c_i <= c_{MLC}\). regression model produces highest posterior density (HPD) intervals limit detection peak. consistent, unbiased estimate model evidence (also known marginal likelihood) also computed. can used evaluate whether Gaussian Lorentzian peaks better fit data.

title: Bayesian modelling and quantification of Raman spectroscopy — serrsBayes-package
code: # simulate some data with known parameter values wavenumbers <- seq(700,1400,by=2) spectra <- matrix(nrow=1, ncol=length(wavenumbers)) peakLocations <- c(840,  960, 1140, 1220, 1290) peakAmplitude <- c(11500, 2500, 4000, 3000, 2500) peakScale <- c(10, 15, 20, 10, 12) signature <- weightedLorentzian(peakLocations, peakScale, peakAmplitude, wavenumbers) baseline <- 1000*cos(wavenumbers/200) + 2*wavenumbers spectra[1,] <- signature + baseline + rnorm(length(wavenumbers),0,200) plot(wavenumbers, spectra[1,], type='l', xlab="Raman offset", ylab="intensity") lines(wavenumbers, baseline, col=2, lty=4) lines(wavenumbers, baseline + signature, col=4, lty=2)   # fit the model using SMC lPriors <- list(scale.mu=log(11.6) - (0.4^2)/2, scale.sd=0.4, bl.smooth=10^11, bl.knots=50,                 beta.mu=5000, beta.sd=5000, noise.sd=200, noise.nu=4)  if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ ## takes approx. 1 minute for 100 SMC iterations with 10,000 particles result <- fitSpectraSMC(wavenumbers, spectra, peakLocations, lPriors) plot.ts(result$ess, xlab="SMC iterations", ylab="ESS")  # sample 200 particles from the posterior distribution samp.idx <- sample.int(length(result$weights), 200, prob=result$weights) plot(wavenumbers, spectra[1,], type='l', xlab="Raman offset", ylab="intensity") for (pt in samp.idx) {   bl.est <- result$basis %*% result$alpha[,1,pt]   lines(wavenumbers, bl.est, col="#C3000009")   lines(wavenumbers, bl.est + result$expFn[pt,], col="#0000C309") } } # }
